items.prose: A maximal margin classifier has $w = (3, 4)$ and $b = -10$, scaled so that its support vectors give $w \cdot x + b = \pm 1$.
items.question: How wide is the empty street, edge to edge? Give one decimal place.

feedback.generic: The street is two margins, and each margin is $1/\lVert w \rVert$.

byKey.margin: You gave one margin, $1/5$. The street spans both sides.
byKey.norm: You gave $\lVert w \rVert = 5$ itself. The width is its reciprocal, twice.
byKey.b: You used $|b|/\lVert w \rVert$, the distance from the origin to the line.

explain.text: $\lVert w \rVert = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, so each margin is 0.2 and the street is 0.4 wide. The intercept only says where the street sits.

items.prose: Five points: $(0, 0)$, $(2, 0)$, $(0, 4)$, $(10, 10)$ and $(12, 10)$. Two centres start at $(0, 0)$ and $(10, 10)$. Do one assign step and one update step.
items.question: What is the inertia of the new groups about the new centres? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Assign, move each centre to its group's mean, then add squared distances.

byKey.before: You measured about the old centres, $0 + 4 + 16 + 0 + 4$. The update moves them first.
byKey.onegroup: You stopped after the first group. The second adds $1 + 1$.

explain.text: The first three points go to $(0, 0)$ and the last two to $(10, 10)$. The new centres are $(2/3, 4/3)$ and $(11, 10)$, and the inertia falls from 24 to $120/9 + 2 \approx 15.33$. An update can only lower it.

items.question: What is $p$ at $(1, 3)$? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Work the hidden units, then $z$, then the logistic function.

byKey.norelu: You kept $h_1 = -1$. The ReLU floors it at 0, so $z = 0$, not $-3$.
byKey.z: You stopped at $z = 0$. The logistic function of 0 is 0.5.

items.prose: A network takes 4 inputs, has one hidden layer of 6 units and an output layer of 3 units.
items.question: How many parameters does it have?

feedback.generic: Each layer: inputs times outputs weights, plus one bias per output unit.

byKey.weights: You counted only weights, $24 + 18$. Add 6 and 3 biases.

explain.text: The hidden layer has $4 \times 6 + 6 = 30$ parameters and the output layer $6 \times 3 + 3 = 21$. That makes 51 in all.

feedback.generic: Switch on every hinge whose knot is below 6.

byKey.nolast: You left out the hinge at 5: $(6 - 5)^+ = 1$ takes 4 off.
byKey.nohinge: You used the line alone. Both hinges are on at 6.

explain.text: At $x = 6$ both hinges are on: $(6 - 2)^+ = 4$ and $(6 - 5)^+ = 1$. So $f(6) = 1 + 12 + 12 - 4 = 21$. The slope there is $2 + 3 - 4 = 1$.

items.prose: On a validation split, an RBF machine scores 0.97 at $\gamma = 0.1$ and 0.97 at $\gamma = 1$, and 0.92 at $\gamma = 10$.
items.question: Which $\gamma$ do you take, and why?

options.text: 0.1: on a tie the longer reach gives a smoother boundary that varies less
1: the middle value is the safest choice between the extremes
options.why: You picked the middle by habit. On a tie the smoother boundary has no cost and less variance.

options.text: 10: the largest value fits the training rows most closely
options.why: You chose by training fit. $\gamma = 10$ validated worst, 0.92.

options.text: Whichever scores higher on the test rows
options.why: You broke the tie on the test rows. Then the test score is no longer an honest report.

feedback.correct: Ties go to the smaller $\gamma$: a smoother boundary.
feedback.generic: Ask which boundary is simpler at equal validation accuracy.

explain.text: Small $\gamma$ means each point reaches far, so the boundary is smooth. At equal validation accuracy the smoother boundary is the safer bet on new rows. The test rows are touched once, after choosing.

items.prose: A learner hits 57% on 400 test days. The base rate of up days in the test period is 53%.
items.question: What is the $t$ statistic of its edge over the base rate? Give two decimal places.

byKey.coin: You tested against a coin: $(0.57 - 0.5)/0.025 = 2.8$. The base rate is 0.53.
byKey.nosqrt: You divided by the variance, not its square root.

explain.text: The standard error is $\sqrt{0.53 \times 0.47 / 400} = 0.0250$, so $t = 0.04 / 0.0250 \approx 1.60$. Against a coin it would look like 2.8. Against the base rate it is not yet evidence.

items.prose: Four assets with distances $d(A, B) = 0.1$, $d(C, D) = 0.4$, $d(A, C) = 0.5$, $d(A, D) = 0.9$, $d(B, C) = 0.6$ and $d(B, D) = 0.7$. Hierarchical clustering merges $A$ with $B$, then $C$ with $D$.
items.question: Under average linkage, at what height do the two pairs merge?

feedback.generic: Average all four cross distances between the pairs.

byKey.single: You took the nearest cross distance, single linkage.
byKey.complete: You took the farthest cross distance, complete linkage.
byKey.mid: You averaged the nearest and farthest only. Average linkage uses all four cross pairs.

explain.text: The cross distances are 0.5, 0.9, 0.6 and 0.7. Their mean, 0.675, is the average-linkage height; single linkage gives 0.5 and complete 0.9. The linkage is a choice that moves the tree.

items.prose: You have 80 rows and 25 features, most of them probably noise, and a binary label.
items.question: Which learner do you fit first?

options.text: A scaled, penalised logistic regression: with few rows per feature, start simple
15-nearest neighbours, since it makes no assumption about shape
options.why: You valued no assumptions. In 25 mostly noisy dimensions, distances are mostly noise.

options.text: A 64-unit network, since it can find any pattern
options.why: You valued capacity. A 64-unit network has about 1,700 parameters for 80 rows.

options.text: An additive model with 10 knots per feature
options.why: You added 300 spline columns to 80 rows. That is far more columns than rows.

feedback.correct: Few rows per feature: start with the simplest learner.

explain.text: 80 rows for 25 features is about 3 rows per feature, the wide row of the table. The simplest learner varies least, and the penalty and scaling keep it stable. Try anything more flexible only as a comparison chosen on validation.

items.prose: A credit model's truth includes a term in leverage times volatility: high leverage is dangerous only when volatility is high.
items.question: Which model cannot capture that, however many knots you give it?

options.text: An RBF support vector machine on both features
options.why: You doubted the kernel. It compares whole points, so it can bend with both features at once.

options.text: A small network with a hidden layer on both features
options.why: You doubted the network. Its hidden units mix both inputs, so it can express a product.

options.text: Logistic regression with a product column added
options.why: You missed the added column. With leverage times volatility as a feature, the product is in the model.

feedback.correct: A sum of one-feature curves cannot express a product.
feedback.generic: Ask which model adds separate effects.

explain.text: In an additive model the effect of leverage is the same at every volatility. A product term needs that effect to change with volatility. Adding the product as a column, or a learner that mixes inputs, fixes it.
